title: Inference cost prioritization - Seven Lakes Analytics discovery
summary: Discovery to understand Seven Lakes' cost sensitivity for high-throughput forecasting inference, evaluate hosted vs dedicated vs private options, and scope a constrained-budget pilot. Discussed per-token pricing impact, batching and KV cache levers, burst traffic at month-end, data residency/PII needs, and security requirements (SOC2 / SSO). Agreed next steps: share model/unit-cost sheet, run a 48-hour hosted benchmark with representative prompts, and follow up with security artifacts and pilot contract template.

hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs for PII and residency

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Reyes (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Alex Chen (Seven Lakes - Head of ML), Maya Ortiz (Seven Lakes - Infra), Liam O'Neal (Seven Lakes - Product)

Summary (auto): Quick intake focused on unit economics and a constrained-budget pilot. Customer has monthly-end burst traffic, PII concerns for some models, and limited budget for PoC. Wants clear levers for cost control (batching, caching, model mix).

Topics: per-token pricing, batching & KV cache, hosted vs dedicated vs private, pilot scope, security requirements.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Reyes: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we appreciate you squeezing us in on the 4th. Quick introductions? I'll start — Jordan, AE at Redwood, and Samir on the call is our systems engineer who helps run pilots and benchmarks.
[00:12] Alex Chen: Alex here, head of ML at Seven Lakes. We run a forecasting infra for retail customers.
[00:16] Maya Ortiz: Maya, infra manager, I own VPCs, security, and on prem hooks.
[00:19] Liam O'Neal: Liam, product.
[00:21] Samir Patel: Samir, Redwood SE, focused on performance and batching.
[00:24] Jordan: Cool. High level — seven lakes, tell us where you're at with models, what you're running, and what's the primary cost pain?

[00:32] Alex: Sure. We have a ensemble — small LMs for enrichment and a 7B-ish autoreg for weekly forecasts. The big problem is month-end spikes; we can go from 50 qps baseline to 400 qps for ~6 hours. Our budget for a pilot is tight — roughly $8k for a 30 day eval window, really more like a short PoC to validate cost per forecast. We're trying to figure out if hosted makes sense or whether we need dedicated pools or an on-prem private setup because of PII and residency.
[01:10] Jordan: Got it. So three concerns: cost/unit, burst handling, and data residency. Typical. On cost per token, we usually talk about effective cost after batching + prefix/KV cache — that can move the per-response number a fair bit compared to list price. Samir, maybe run through an example?
[01:28] Samir: Yeah, quick example. If you're doing single-shot forecasting prompts at 1k tokens, naive per-token billing looks bad. But if we use request-level batching with a batch size tuned to keep latency within your SLO and enable KV cache for repeated prefixes, your effective tokens billed per infer can fall 25-60% depending on prompt overlap. With our hosted defaults we can do continuous batching and have autoscaling to handle bursts — but there are tradeoffs.
[01:58] Alex: When you say KV cache, are you caching client data? We have PII in prompts, can't store that persistently.
[02:06] Samir: Good question. We do prefix/KV cache that's configurable — for PII you'd opt for in-memory ephemeral caches with TTL and no persistence to disk. For private deployments we can ensure cache stays in your VPC, KMS-protected keys.
[02:20] Maya: That matters. Our compliance team will flag anything persisted outside our control.
[02:25] Jordan: Totally. For that reason private or dedicated is common. Dedicated gives isolated GPUs and the option to pin instances in a region for residency. Private (VPC or on-prem) lets you keep everything under your KMS/HSM. Hosted can work if you accept ephemeral memory and contractual residency constraints.
[02:44] Liam: Curious — price delta between hosted and dedicated? If we commit to a monthly reserved capacity what's the unit impact?
[02:51] Jordan: There are two dimensions: unit price (per-token/embedding) and effective units consumed (post-batching/cache). Dedicated typically lowers the per-token list price and gives predictable throughput for burst capacity. For example (ballpark) hosted list price for the 7B-like model might be $0.0009/token, dedicated lanes could push that to $0.0006/token depending on commit size. But your effective cost depends on how much batching and reuse you achieve.
[03:21] Alex: Those are helpful numbers. With our budget constraints — we can't do a big reserved commit right away. We're realistically looking at a short pilot with hosted but want to know if the numbers will map to dedicated when we scale.
[03:33] Samir: We often do that — run a hosted benchmark to understand the effective unit and then model the dedicated projection. I can prepare a spreadsheet that simulates different batching configs and KV cache hit rates — we will include a conservative, expected, and optimistic column.
[03:47] Maya: When you simulate kv hit rates, what's realistic for us? Our prompts change per customer but many prefixes are the same like header/context.
[03:55] Samir: If you have stable prefixes you can expect 20–40% token savings quickly; if prompts are almost identical you'll see 50%+. But if each request is unique the gains drop. For your forecasting use-case, we usually see 30–45% because the model prompt includes a fixed header + variable data rows.
[04:15] Alex: That matches our intuition. Month-end spikes though, we worry about latency — can't degrade SLA.
[04:21] Jordan: Right, that's where multi-tier routing and fallback policies help. You can route critical traffic to dedicated lanes and best-effort to hosted, or set thresholds that fall back to a smaller model when latency threatens SLA.
[04:37] Liam: Fallbacks are interesting — are those automatic? We don't want to manage policies in code if possible.
[04:42] Samir: We can manage via route policies in the console. You set your latency SLOs and cost ceilings, and the routing engine will obey those, falling back to compatible model variants or alternate capacity. It can be autonomous or managed with manual overrides.
[04:56] Maya: About the pilot — we need a 48-hour run that captures a simulated month-end spike, to see cost/latency math. Could Redwood run that on hosted?
[05:05] Samir: Yes. Hosted is easiest for a quick benchmark. We'll need your prompt set, representative throughput schedule, and a metric plan. We'll run a 48-hour continuous run and provide per-token breakdowns, batching stats, cache hit rates, and latency percentiles.
[05:21] Alex: Sounds good. We can extract a week's worth of traffic and a synthetic month-end pattern.
[05:26] Jordan: Perfect. I'll send the cost spreadsheet and a pilot template. Also, quick compliance check — are you expecting SOC2 or ISO artifacts?
[05:34] Maya: SOC2 is mandatory, and SSO via SAML is required. Also, we need the ability to rotate keys with our KMS for private deployments.
[05:44] Samir: We can share SOC2 report and SAML docs. For KMS, in private deployments you can bring your own keys and we don't store secrets. For hosted there are managed key options with limited rotation windows, but for strict compliance private is recommended.
[05:59] Alex: How about network residency — some customers demand EU-only. Can dedicated pools be region pinned?
[06:06] Jordan: Yes, dedicated pools can be pinned to a region and the control plane supports region constraints. Private VPC/on-prem obviously gives full control.
[06:14] Liam: On cost — is there a blunt way to estimate per-forecast cost? We have ~600 tokens per forecast median.
[06:21] Samir: Rough calc: list price * tokens * (1 - savings_from_batch_cache). Example: $0.0009/token * 600 tokens = $0.54 naive. If you get 35% savings from batch+cache, effective = $0.35. That's before any dedicated discount or reserved commit.
[06:42] Alex: So for our month-end peak of 400 qps sustained for 6 hours, what is the burn?
[06:49] Samir: If every request is 600 tokens and naive pricing: 400 qps * 3600 sec/hour * 6 hours * 600 tokens * $0.0009/token = huge number — better to calculate tokens/sec. But practically you'll rely on batching during bursts; effective tokens per request will go down. We'll produce a worked example in the spreadsheet.
[07:10] Jordan: We'll also model burst capacity and reserve lanes; if you commit to a modest monthly baseline we can allow burst overage with negotiated rates.
[07:19] Maya: Important — encryption at rest and audit logs. For compliance we need to show audit trails of requests and who accessed them.
[07:27] Samir: Audit logs are available across hosted/dedicated/private. For hosted we retain per token logs per contract; for private you control retention. We can also wire logs into your SIEM.
[07:36] Alex: Good. One more thing — how do you treat embeddings vs generation pricing? We use both for product A.
[07:43] Jordan: Embeddings are priced separately per embedding unit and tend to be cheaper per operation but different size. We'll include separate lanes in the sheet.
[07:50] Liam: Ok. Sequence for pilot?
[07:52] Jordan: Step 1: you send prompt set + traffic profile. Step 2: we run 48h hosted benchmark. Step 3: review results, and we produce dedicated projection and pilot pricing. Step 4: security artifacts exchanged and pilot contract.
[08:07] Alex: Timeline — if we send artifacts by Monday, can we get the benchmark run next week?
[08:12] Samir: Yes, we can schedule as early as Tuesday next week assuming the prompt set is ready.
[08:17] Maya: Are there any upfront costs for the run?
[08:20] Jordan: Usually the benchmark is complimentary for qualified pilots. If you need an extended dedicated trial there may be a nominal charge. We'll call that out.
[08:30] Alex: Competitors — we've spoken to Vendor X and Y, they gave similar numbers but lacked the cache/batching observability. That's why we wanted to talk to Redwood.
[08:41] Samir: Observability is a focus — token-level cost, tracing, per-route dashboards.
[08:47] Liam: Quick nit: can we limit model size to reduce cost and only route tricky queries to the larger model?
[08:53] Samir: Yes, route rules + model mix. You can do staged routing: run majority on a smaller 3B model and escalate to 7B for tails, or use reranking to keep quality.
[09:04] Alex: Is there a recommended threshold for switching? e.g., if confidence < 0.6 route to larger model?
[09:10] Samir: That's a common policy. We support signals-based routing: confidence, latency, cost. We'll include sample policies.
[09:18] Jordan: Any blockers from your side to execute the pilot?
[09:21] Maya: SOC2 review timeline tends to be the blocker — but for an initial hosted run we think we can keep data anonymized. We need to sign an SA and NAC then proceed.
[09:31] Jordan: We'll send the SA template.
[09:33] Alex: Perfect.
[09:35] Liam: OK great, let's do it.
[09:37] Jordan: Recap briefly — Jordan to send cost spreadsheet and pilot template, Samir to draft benchmark plan, Seven Lakes to provide prompt set and traffic profile, exchange SOC2 and SSO docs. Follow-up call next Friday to review results.
[09:52] Alex: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[09:55] Maya: Thanks.
[09:56] Jordan: Thanks all.

Notes (auto): There were a few transcription artifacts ("k v cache" sometimes transcribed as KVM cache), and a vendor name shortened to Vendor X. Customer emphasized month-end bursts and PII concerns; agreed to host benchmark.
